# Visualizing Robot Positioning Accuracy and Repeatability in 3D

## 1. Overview

Three principal methods appear in the published literature for showing a robot's positioning accuracy and repeatability in three dimensions: **(1) error ellipsoids** (the stochastic ellipsoid method), **(2) probabilistic workspace maps**, and **(3) Jacobian-based confidence volumes along a path or trajectory**. Each can be computed from physical measurements, from modeled parameter uncertainties, or from both. The table below summarizes these methods, their mathematical basis, published protocols, and supporting software.

Orientation shows principal error directions, semi-axis lengths show directional dispersion, and volume summarizes overall uncertainty. | From measured or simulated Cartesian errors, compute covariance Σ and eigendecompose it as Σ = VDVᵀ. Eigenvectors give principal directions and eigenvalues λ_j give variances. A 3σ ellipsoid has semi-axes a_j = 3√λ_j. Joint-space uncertainty can also be propagated into task space through the Jacobian. (makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 5-7, issametova2026reliabilityinrobotics pages 13-15, sinha2019computingrobustinverse pages 3-4) | **Measured:** command the same pose repeatedly, record 3D TCP coordinates, subtract their mean, and estimate Σ. ## 2. Error Ellipsoids (Stochastic Ellipsoid Method)

### 2.1 Mathematical Construction

The stochastic ellipsoid method represents positioning uncertainty at a given robot configuration as a three-dimensional confidence region derived from the covariance of end-effector position errors. Makhambetov et al. describe the procedure: "The displacement samples are calculated as Δp = p_noisy − p_nom, then their covariance matrix Σ is eigendecomposed as Σ = VDVᵀ. The eigenvectors in V define the principal directions of the uncertainty ellipsoid, while the eigenvalues λ_j represent variances along those directions. A 3σ ellipsoid uses semi-axis lengths a_j = 3√λ_j" (makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 5-7). The volume of this ellipsoid, (4/3)π∏a_j, provides a scalar summary of total uncertainty while retaining directional information that a single RMS number discards (makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 5-7).

Alternatively, the ellipsoid can be computed analytically from the kinematic Jacobian. Issametova et al. explain: "Robot parameter or drive-error uncertainties are represented by a covariance matrix Σ_q and propagated through the kinematic Jacobian, using the relationship Σ_X = J_q Σ_q J_qᵀ" (issametova2026reliabilityinrobotics pages 48-49). The 3×3 translational block of Σ_X is then eigendecomposed to obtain the ellipsoid. For task-space error, Sinha and Chakraborty (preprint) show that joint-space uncertainty propagated through the position Jacobian J_p yields "δXᵀ(J_p J_pᵀ)⁻¹δX ≤ c," which "geometrically describes an ellipsoid" of position errors at the end-effector (sinha2019computingrobustinverse pages 3-4).

### 2.2 Protocol and Validation

Issametova et al. validated the ellipsoid approach experimentally on a **FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L**, measuring at "25 workspace points and 50 repeated trials per point, with a laser tracker accurate to about 0.01 mm" (issametova2026reliabilityinrobotics pages 37-39). They found that analytical and Monte Carlo ellipsoids agreed within 1–3% for compact and medium configurations, but diverged by 7–10% for elongated configurations where nonlinear kinematics dominate: "Experimental error ellipsoids showed that the major axis could be displaced by up to 10–11° relative to model predictions, with variance up to 20% higher than predicted" (issametova2026reliabilityinrobotics pages 45-48). This is a peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.3390/math14030580).

Makhambetov et al. used a purely computational approach on a generic 6-DOF manipulator with "N = 10,000 trials across 50 workspace configurations" and rendered 3σ error ellipsoids through a Unity3D Digital Twin (makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 1-2). Their ellipsoids were anisotropic, with the longest axis primarily vertical due to gravitational elastic deformation (makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 11-14). This is a peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.3390/electronics15143095) but contains no physical measurement validation; the authors note that "future work will compare them with measured end-effector scatter using a laser tracker" (makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 16-17).

Rezala and Arbaoui used the stochastic ellipsoid method to analyze repeatability errors caused by joint friction variations, noting that "the stochastic ellipsoid method is able to generate repeatability predictions for the entire workspace" (rezala2022analysisrandoncauses pages 2-4). This is a peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.5829/ije.2022.35.02b.21).

### 2.3 How to Repeat for Low-Cost Arms

For the AgileX PiPER or SO-101, one can command the arm to the same pose repeatedly (≥30 cycles per ISO 9283), record the TCP position using an AprilTag-based external camera system or a dial indicator, compute the 3×3 position covariance from the scatter, and eigendecompose it to obtain the ellipsoid axes and semi-lengths. This requires no laser tracker; the user's existing fixed cameras and AprilTags can serve as the measurement system, though with lower absolute accuracy than a laser tracker. **No published study has applied error ellipsoid analysis specifically to AgileX PiPER, SO-101, or comparable sub-$2,000 arms.**

## 3. Probabilistic Workspace Maps

### 3.1 Monte Carlo Workspace Characterization

Workspace maps extend single-point ellipsoid analysis to the entire reachable space. Makhambetov et al. constructed a "probabilistic workspace map using 3,000 uniformly sampled configurations within joint limits and 500 trials per point, totaling 1,500,000 forward-kinematics evaluations" (makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 5-7). The result is a color-coded 3D point cloud: "green denotes RMS error below 5 mm, yellow 5–15 mm, and red above 15 mm" (makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 9-11). The maps reveal that "central workspace corresponds to compact configurations" with low error, while "reliability decreases toward workspace boundaries" (issametova2026reliabilityinrobotics pages 45-48).

Issametova et al. constructed a geometric-reliability map for the FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L, defining reliability as the probability that the end-effector lands within a tolerance region. They report "approximately 0.98 in central workspace regions associated with compact configurations" declining to "approximately 0.70 in peripheral zones" (issametova2026reliabilityinrobotics pages 45-48). This was computed from both analytical (Jacobian-based) and Monte Carlo methods, peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.3390/math14030580).

### 3.2 Measurement-Based Workspace Maps

Chen applied the ISO 9283 protocol to the **Baxter** robot to generate "a 3D mapping of repeatability at different heights," finding that "repeatability generally deteriorated as the target moved farther from the robot" (chen2015applicationofthe pages 14-18). The protocol tested 15 target locations at three heights, with 30 cycles per experiment repeated 30 times (900 measurements per location), using 3D dial gauges with 0.005 mm accuracy (chen2015applicationofthea pages 14-18, chen2015applicationofthe pages 14-18). This is a thesis (2015).

### 3.3 ISO 9283 Protocol Summary

The ISO 9283 standard prescribes the canonical measurement protocol. A test cube is placed in the most-used workspace region with edges parallel to the robot base coordinates. Five poses (P1–P5) lie on a diagonal test plane, P1 at the cube center and P2–P5 near diagonal corners. The robot visits these poses in unidirectional order through 30 cycles at each of three speeds (10%, 50%, 100% of rated velocity) and 100% rated payload. Position repeatability is computed as "RP_l = mean distance from the barycentre plus three standard deviations" (chen2015applicationofthe pages 18-23, chen2015applicationofthea pages 18-23). This protocol has been applied with various measurement tools including laser trackers (Faro Vantage, accuracy ±0.009 mm), contact gauges, and vision systems (pollak2023simulationdesignand pages 2-4, płaczek2018testingofan pages 3-5).

## 4. Jacobian-Based Confidence Volumes and Error Along a Path

### 4.1 The Probabilistic Product-of-Exponentials (PPOE) Model

Meyer et al. presented the PPOE model at IROS 2022, which "does not only consider the robot's deterministic geometry but additionally models time-varying and configuration-dependent errors in a probabilistic way" (meyer2022theprobabilisticrobot pages 1-2). The model propagates errors along the kinematic chain using Lie-group operations and computes their influence on the end-effector pose. It was validated on a **Kinova Jaco2** arm, where "PPOE-based 2D estimation achieved mean lateral errors of 0.29 ± 0.15 cm and 0.50 ± 0.25 cm" compared with forward kinematics alone at "0.82 ± 0.49 cm and 1.48 ± 0.38 cm" (meyer2022theprobabilisticrobot pages 6-8). This is a peer-reviewed IEEE conference paper (DOI: 10.1109/IROS47612.2022.9981399).

### 4.2 pytransform3d: An Open-Source Uncertainty Visualization Library

The Python library pytransform3d provides the most accessible implementation for low-cost arm users. Fabisch and Popescu describe its uncertainty module: it "models uncertain rigid transformations using a transformation-matrix mean and a 6×6 covariance matrix over exponential coordinates" and supports "composition, inversion, and fusion of uncertain transformations" (fabisch2026newfeaturesof pages 9-10). Key functions include `concat_locally_uncertain_transforms(A2B, B2C, cov_A, cov_B)` for propagating joint-displacement covariances, and `adjoint_from_transform(A2B)` for transferring covariance between frames (fabisch2026newfeaturesof pages 12-13). The library renders "an equiprobable projected 6D pose hyperellipsoid at configurable kσ intervals in 3D; the example describes a 3σ hyperellipsoid, corresponding to 99.7% probability" (fabisch2026newfeaturesof pages 9-10). Importantly, the authors note that "an ellipsoid is not an appropriate representation" for all cases because rotation-translation coupling can produce banana-shaped distributions rather than ordinary ellipsoids (fabisch2026newfeaturesof pages 10-12). The library supports URDF loading through `UrdfTransformManager` and visualization through both Matplotlib and Open3D (fabisch2026newfeaturesof pages 10-12, fabisch2026newfeaturesof pages 6-9). This is a peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.3389/frobt.2026.1860457).

### 4.3 Path-Error Visualization

For error along a path, Issametova et al. describe evaluating the Jacobian-based reliability calculation "along θ(t), allowing reliability, variance, or error to be plotted against path position or time; trajectory planners can constrain R(θ(t)) to remain above a required threshold" (issametova2026reliabilityinrobotics pages 48-49). ISO 9283 also defines path accuracy and path repeatability as separate criteria measured by recording the continuous trajectory and comparing it with the commanded path (pollak2023simulationdesignand pages 2-4).

## 5. Calibration Context: Comparative Results Across Arm Models

While this review focuses on visualization rather than calibration, several papers provide comparative positioning-accuracy results that establish the baseline these visualizations would display:

- **FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L**: Positioning error increased from 0.018 mm (first 3 months) to 0.041 mm (last 3 months) in operational monitoring (issametova2026reliabilityinrobotics pages 45-48).
- **Kinova Jaco2**: Forward kinematics error of 0.82–1.48 cm, reduced to 0.29–0.50 cm with PPOE-based sensor fusion using AprilTags (meyer2022theprobabilisticrobot pages 6-8).
- **Franka Panda**: Mean absolute positioning error reduced from ~10 mm to 0.24–0.35 mm by MUKCa calibration; Kinova Gen3Lite improved from 5.99 mm to 2.66 mm, with remaining error attributed to "joint backlash in planetary gearboxes" (franzese2025mukcaaccurateand pages 4-6). This is a preprint (DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2503.12584).
- **Generic 7-DOF arm** (Wyk et al., preprint): Bayesian remastering using a motion capture system reduced "the average robot positioning error to 0.26 mm" and the "average absolute positioning error" from over 4 mm (Vernier method) to "within 1.5 mm" with Bayesian zero-offset optimization (wyk2019efficientlyimprovingand pages 3-4, wyk2019efficientlyimprovingand pages 7-8).
- **Kuka KR 16-2**: Tested per PN-EN 9283 with a Faro Vantage laser tracker (accuracy ±0.009 mm), 30 measurements per test configuration, robot warmed up with a 40-minute cycle (płaczek2018testingofan pages 3-5).
- **Panasonic TM-2000**: ISO 9283 contact-measurement protocol, 1200 mm ISO cube, 5 points, 30 cycles, 50% max speed, 3 kg load, ambient 20–22°C (pollak2023simulationdesignand pages 1-2, pollak2023simulationdesignand pages 7-9).

**No published study was found that applies error ellipsoid analysis, probabilistic workspace mapping, or ISO 9283 repeatability testing specifically to the AgileX PiPER, SO-101, or comparable sub-$200 leader-follower arms.** The closest analogue is the Kinova Gen3Lite (~$5,000), which exhibited substantial backlash-related positioning error around 2–6 mm (franzese2025mukcaaccurateand pages 4-6). Low-cost arms with hobby servos and planetary gearboxes are expected to show similar or larger non-Gaussian error distributions due to backlash and compliance.

## 7. Practical Recommendations for Low-Cost Arms

For the user's AgileX PiPER and SO-101 arms with AprilTag-based measurement:

1. **Collect repeated TCP measurements** at ≥5 workspace locations following the ISO 9283 protocol (30 cycles per location, unidirectional approach). AprilTags detected by the fixed cameras provide the external position reference. Record raw 3D coordinates.

2. **Compute error ellipsoids** at each location using NumPy: subtract the mean, form the 3×3 covariance matrix, and eigendecompose. Plot 3σ ellipsoids using Matplotlib or Open3D. The eigenvalues reveal whether error is isotropic or dominated by a particular direction (e.g., gravity-axis compliance).

3. **Build a workspace map** by repeating step 1 across a grid of reachable locations. Color-code each point by its RMS repeatability and render as a 3D scatter plot. This requires no laser tracker and can be performed with the existing camera infrastructure.

4. **Use pytransform3d** for Jacobian-based propagation if a URDF model of the arm is available. The `concat_locally_uncertain_transforms` function propagates joint-angle covariances through the kinematic chain, and the projected hyperellipsoid visualization shows the resulting end-effector uncertainty (fabisch2026newfeaturesof pages 9-10, fabisch2026newfeaturesof pages 12-13).

5. **Plot path error** by commanding a straight-line or circular trajectory, recording the measured TCP path at high frequency, and computing cross-track and along-track deviations as a function of path parameter. ISO 9283 path repeatability compares the envelope of deviations across multiple traversals (pollak2023simulationdesignand pages 2-4).

## 8. Gaps in Published Evidence

- No peer-reviewed study applies error ellipsoid or probabilistic workspace mapping to the AgileX PiPER, SO-101, or comparable sub-$200 robot arms.
- No published software provides a turnkey, one-click repeatability map function; assembly from numerical primitives is required (fabisch2026newfeaturesof pages 9-10, makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 16-17).
- The Makhambetov et al. (2026) workspace maps and error ellipsoids are simulation-only and have not been validated against physical measurements (makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 16-17).
- Path-error visualization (error plotted continuously along a trajectory rather than at discrete points) is described mathematically but not demonstrated with dedicated software in the retrieved literature (issametova2026reliabilityinrobotics pages 48-49).
- The Sinha and Chakraborty (2019) robust IK work with error ellipsoids is a preprint (DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.1910.10852) and has not appeared in a peer-reviewed venue (sinha2019computingrobustinverse pages 3-4).
- The Franzese et al. (2025) MUKCa calibration study for Franka, KUKA, and Kinova is a preprint (DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2503.12584) (franzese2025mukcaaccurateand pages 4-6).

# Visualizing Robot Positioning Accuracy and Repeatability in 3D

## 1. Overview

Three principal methods appear in the published literature for showing a robot's positioning accuracy and repeatability in three dimensions: **(1) error ellipsoids** (the stochastic ellipsoid method), **(2) probabilistic workspace maps**, and **(3) Jacobian-based confidence volumes along a path or trajectory**. Each can be computed from physical measurements, from modeled parameter uncertainties, or from both. The table below summarizes these methods, their mathematical basis, published protocols, and supporting software.

| Method | What is Visualized | Mathematical Basis | Protocol Detail | Software/Tools | Key Reference (with DOI) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Error ellipsoids (stochastic ellipsoid method)** | A 3D confidence region around the nominal or mean TCP position. Orientation shows principal error directions, semi-axis lengths show directional dispersion, and volume summarizes overall uncertainty. | From measured or simulated Cartesian errors, compute covariance Σ and eigendecompose it as Σ = VDVᵀ. Eigenvectors give principal directions and eigenvalues λ_j give variances. A 3σ ellipsoid has semi-axes a_j = 3√λ_j. Joint-space uncertainty can also be propagated into task space through the Jacobian. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000030) | **Measured:** command the same pose repeatedly, record 3D TCP coordinates, subtract their mean, and estimate Σ. Issametova et al. tested a FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L at 25 workspace points with 50 trials per point using a laser tracker accurate to about 0.01 mm. **Modeled:** Makhambetov et al. used 10,000 Monte Carlo trials at each of 50 configurations; that study was simulation-only and deferred physical validation. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000019) | NumPy/SciPy or MATLAB for covariance and eigendecomposition; Matplotlib, Plotly, Open3D, or Unity3D for rendering. The cited digital twin used MATLAB and Unity3D. | Makhambetov et al. (2026), [DOI 10.3390/electronics15143095](https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15143095); Issametova et al. (2026), [DOI 10.3390/math14030580](https://doi.org/10.3390/math14030580); Rezala and Arbaoui (2022), [DOI 10.5829/ije.2022.35.02b.21](https://doi.org/10.5829/ije.2022.35.02b.21); Sinha and Chakraborty (**preprint**, 2019), [DOI 10.48550/arXiv.1910.10852](https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.1910.10852). (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000035) |
| **Probabilistic workspace maps (Monte Carlo or repeated measurements)** | A color-coded 3D point cloud, voxel map, or sliced heat map over the reachable workspace. Each location can encode RMS error, P95 error, ellipsoid volume, ISO repeatability, or probability of remaining inside a task tolerance. | At each workspace location, generate or measure an error distribution and calculate RMS, P95, covariance, or reliability R = P(X ∈ Ω). Display measured samples directly or interpolate them only when spatial sampling is sufficiently dense. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014) | Makhambetov et al. sampled **3,000 configurations with 500 trials each**, totaling 1.5 million forward-kinematics evaluations. Points were green below 5 mm RMS, yellow from 5–15 mm, and red above 15 mm. Issametova et al. mapped successful-positioning probability for a FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L, reporting about 0.98 centrally and 0.70 near peripheral configurations. A hardware alternative is to repeat an ISO-style pose test across a grid of reachable points. (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000039) | MATLAB or Python for Monte Carlo; Plotly, Open3D, or PyVista for point clouds and slices; Unity3D for an interactive digital twin. RoboDK can generate nominal configurations, but the cited evidence does not establish a built-in statistical repeatability-map function. | Makhambetov et al. (2026), [DOI 10.3390/electronics15143095](https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15143095); Issametova et al. (2026), [DOI 10.3390/math14030580](https://doi.org/10.3390/math14030580). (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000039) |
| **Jacobian-based propagation and confidence volumes along a path** | Configuration-dependent confidence volumes at sampled trajectory poses, plus plots of cross-track error, along-track error, orientation error, RMS, or tolerance probability versus time or arc length. Full SE(3) uncertainty may project into a curved or banana-shaped volume rather than a true Cartesian ellipsoid. | Linearized propagation uses δX ≈ J_qδq and Σ_X = J_qΣ_qJ_qᵀ. For measured paths, time-align commanded and measured poses, compute their relative transform, and resolve translation into tangent and normal components. A 6×6 SE(3) covariance can be transported between frames with the adjoint and projected into 3D. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000016) | Estimate Σ_q from stationary joint logs, encoder specifications, calibration residuals, or fitted parameter uncertainty. Evaluate the Jacobian and propagate covariance at every path sample, then validate with repeated externally measured runs. ISO 9283-style pose testing uses five poses on a diagonal plane and 30 cycles per speed/payload condition. Meyer et al. demonstrated configuration-dependent covariance on a Kinova Jaco2 using AprilTags and VICON ground truth at 9 and 29 configurations. (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000042) | **pytransform3d** supports SE(3) covariance composition, inversion, adjoint frame changes, URDF kinematics, and projected 6D confidence hyperellipsoids through Matplotlib or Open3D. ROS/tf and RViz can display frames, paths, markers, and custom ellipsoid meshes. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000044) | Fabisch and Popescu (2026), [DOI 10.3389/frobt.2026.1860457](https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2026.1860457); Meyer et al., IROS 2022, [DOI 10.1109/IROS47612.2022.9981399](https://doi.org/10.1109/iros47612.2022.9981399). (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029) |


*Table: Comparison of three reproducible approaches for visualizing manipulator accuracy and repeatability, including their mathematics, experimental protocols, software, and supporting literature.*

## 2. Error Ellipsoids (Stochastic Ellipsoid Method)

### 2.1 Mathematical Construction

The stochastic ellipsoid method represents positioning uncertainty at a given robot configuration as a three-dimensional confidence region derived from the covariance of end-effector position errors. Makhambetov et al. describe the procedure: "The displacement samples are calculated as Δp = p_noisy − p_nom, then their covariance matrix Σ is eigendecomposed as Σ = VDVᵀ. The eigenvectors in V define the principal directions of the uncertainty ellipsoid, while the eigenvalues λ_j represent variances along those directions. A 3σ ellipsoid uses semi-axis lengths a_j = 3√λ_j" (pqac-00000012). The volume of this ellipsoid, (4/3)π∏a_j, provides a scalar summary of total uncertainty while retaining directional information that a single RMS number discards (pqac-00000012).

Alternatively, the ellipsoid can be computed analytically from the kinematic Jacobian. Issametova et al. explain: "Robot parameter or drive-error uncertainties are represented by a covariance matrix Σ_q and propagated through the kinematic Jacobian, using the relationship Σ_X = J_q Σ_q J_qᵀ" (pqac-00000002). The 3×3 translational block of Σ_X is then eigendecomposed to obtain the ellipsoid. For task-space error, Sinha and Chakraborty (preprint) show that joint-space uncertainty propagated through the position Jacobian J_p yields "δXᵀ(J_p J_pᵀ)⁻¹δX ≤ c," which "geometrically describes an ellipsoid" of position errors at the end-effector (pqac-00000030).

### 2.2 Protocol and Validation

Issametova et al. validated the ellipsoid approach experimentally on a **FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L**, measuring at "25 workspace points and 50 repeated trials per point, with a laser tracker accurate to about 0.01 mm" (pqac-00000015). They found that analytical and Monte Carlo ellipsoids agreed within 1–3% for compact and medium configurations, but diverged by 7–10% for elongated configurations where nonlinear kinematics dominate: "Experimental error ellipsoids showed that the major axis could be displaced by up to 10–11° relative to model predictions, with variance up to 20% higher than predicted" (pqac-00000039). This is a peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.3390/math14030580).

Makhambetov et al. used a purely computational approach on a generic 6-DOF manipulator with "N = 10,000 trials across 50 workspace configurations" and rendered 3σ error ellipsoids through a Unity3D Digital Twin (pqac-00000031). Their ellipsoids were anisotropic, with the longest axis primarily vertical due to gravitational elastic deformation (pqac-00000014). This is a peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.3390/electronics15143095) but contains no physical measurement validation; the authors note that "future work will compare them with measured end-effector scatter using a laser tracker" (pqac-00000019).

Rezala and Arbaoui used the stochastic ellipsoid method to analyze repeatability errors caused by joint friction variations, noting that "the stochastic ellipsoid method is able to generate repeatability predictions for the entire workspace" (pqac-00000035). This is a peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.5829/ije.2022.35.02b.21).

### 2.3 How to Repeat for Low-Cost Arms

For the AgileX PiPER or SO-101, one can command the arm to the same pose repeatedly (≥30 cycles per ISO 9283), record the TCP position using an AprilTag-based external camera system or a dial indicator, compute the 3×3 position covariance from the scatter, and eigendecompose it to obtain the ellipsoid axes and semi-lengths. This requires no laser tracker; the user's existing fixed cameras and AprilTags can serve as the measurement system, though with lower absolute accuracy than a laser tracker. **No published study has applied error ellipsoid analysis specifically to AgileX PiPER, SO-101, or comparable sub-$2,000 arms.**

## 3. Probabilistic Workspace Maps

### 3.1 Monte Carlo Workspace Characterization

Workspace maps extend single-point ellipsoid analysis to the entire reachable space. Makhambetov et al. constructed a "probabilistic workspace map using 3,000 uniformly sampled configurations within joint limits and 500 trials per point, totaling 1,500,000 forward-kinematics evaluations" (pqac-00000012). The result is a color-coded 3D point cloud: "green denotes RMS error below 5 mm, yellow 5–15 mm, and red above 15 mm" (pqac-00000013). The maps reveal that "central workspace corresponds to compact configurations" with low error, while "reliability decreases toward workspace boundaries" (pqac-00000018).

Issametova et al. constructed a geometric-reliability map for the FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L, defining reliability as the probability that the end-effector lands within a tolerance region. They report "approximately 0.98 in central workspace regions associated with compact configurations" declining to "approximately 0.70 in peripheral zones" (pqac-00000039). This was computed from both analytical (Jacobian-based) and Monte Carlo methods, peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.3390/math14030580).

### 3.2 Measurement-Based Workspace Maps

Chen applied the ISO 9283 protocol to the **Baxter** robot to generate "a 3D mapping of repeatability at different heights," finding that "repeatability generally deteriorated as the target moved farther from the robot" (pqac-00000000). The protocol tested 15 target locations at three heights, with 30 cycles per experiment repeated 30 times (900 measurements per location), using 3D dial gauges with 0.005 mm accuracy (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000027). This is a thesis (2015).

### 3.3 ISO 9283 Protocol Summary

The ISO 9283 standard prescribes the canonical measurement protocol. A test cube is placed in the most-used workspace region with edges parallel to the robot base coordinates. Five poses (P1–P5) lie on a diagonal test plane, P1 at the cube center and P2–P5 near diagonal corners. The robot visits these poses in unidirectional order through 30 cycles at each of three speeds (10%, 50%, 100% of rated velocity) and 100% rated payload. Position repeatability is computed as "RP_l = mean distance from the barycentre plus three standard deviations" (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000023). This protocol has been applied with various measurement tools including laser trackers (Faro Vantage, accuracy ±0.009 mm), contact gauges, and vision systems (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021).

## 4. Jacobian-Based Confidence Volumes and Error Along a Path

### 4.1 The Probabilistic Product-of-Exponentials (PPOE) Model

Meyer et al. presented the PPOE model at IROS 2022, which "does not only consider the robot's deterministic geometry but additionally models time-varying and configuration-dependent errors in a probabilistic way" (pqac-00000028). The model propagates errors along the kinematic chain using Lie-group operations and computes their influence on the end-effector pose. It was validated on a **Kinova Jaco2** arm, where "PPOE-based 2D estimation achieved mean lateral errors of 0.29 ± 0.15 cm and 0.50 ± 0.25 cm" compared with forward kinematics alone at "0.82 ± 0.49 cm and 1.48 ± 0.38 cm" (pqac-00000042). This is a peer-reviewed IEEE conference paper (DOI: 10.1109/IROS47612.2022.9981399).

### 4.2 pytransform3d: An Open-Source Uncertainty Visualization Library

The Python library pytransform3d provides the most accessible implementation for low-cost arm users. Fabisch and Popescu describe its uncertainty module: it "models uncertain rigid transformations using a transformation-matrix mean and a 6×6 covariance matrix over exponential coordinates" and supports "composition, inversion, and fusion of uncertain transformations" (pqac-00000008). Key functions include `concat_locally_uncertain_transforms(A2B, B2C, cov_A, cov_B)` for propagating joint-displacement covariances, and `adjoint_from_transform(A2B)` for transferring covariance between frames (pqac-00000011). The library renders "an equiprobable projected 6D pose hyperellipsoid at configurable kσ intervals in 3D; the example describes a 3σ hyperellipsoid, corresponding to 99.7% probability" (pqac-00000008). Importantly, the authors note that "an ellipsoid is not an appropriate representation" for all cases because rotation-translation coupling can produce banana-shaped distributions rather than ordinary ellipsoids (pqac-00000009). The library supports URDF loading through `UrdfTransformManager` and visualization through both Matplotlib and Open3D (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). This is a peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.3389/frobt.2026.1860457).

### 4.3 Path-Error Visualization

For error along a path, Issametova et al. describe evaluating the Jacobian-based reliability calculation "along θ(t), allowing reliability, variance, or error to be plotted against path position or time; trajectory planners can constrain R(θ(t)) to remain above a required threshold" (pqac-00000002). ISO 9283 also defines path accuracy and path repeatability as separate criteria measured by recording the continuous trajectory and comparing it with the commanded path (pqac-00000020).

## 5. Calibration Context: Comparative Results Across Arm Models

While this review focuses on visualization rather than calibration, several papers provide comparative positioning-accuracy results that establish the baseline these visualizations would display:

- **FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L**: Positioning error increased from 0.018 mm (first 3 months) to 0.041 mm (last 3 months) in operational monitoring (pqac-00000039).
- **Kinova Jaco2**: Forward kinematics error of 0.82–1.48 cm, reduced to 0.29–0.50 cm with PPOE-based sensor fusion using AprilTags (pqac-00000042).
- **Franka Panda**: Mean absolute positioning error reduced from ~10 mm to 0.24–0.35 mm by MUKCa calibration; Kinova Gen3Lite improved from 5.99 mm to 2.66 mm, with remaining error attributed to "joint backlash in planetary gearboxes" (pqac-00000041). This is a preprint (DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2503.12584).
- **Generic 7-DOF arm** (Wyk et al., preprint): Bayesian remastering using a motion capture system reduced "the average robot positioning error to 0.26 mm" and the "average absolute positioning error" from over 4 mm (Vernier method) to "within 1.5 mm" with Bayesian zero-offset optimization (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034).
- **Kuka KR 16-2**: Tested per PN-EN 9283 with a Faro Vantage laser tracker (accuracy ±0.009 mm), 30 measurements per test configuration, robot warmed up with a 40-minute cycle (pqac-00000021).
- **Panasonic TM-2000**: ISO 9283 contact-measurement protocol, 1200 mm ISO cube, 5 points, 30 cycles, 50% max speed, 3 kg load, ambient 20–22°C (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026).

**No published study was found that applies error ellipsoid analysis, probabilistic workspace mapping, or ISO 9283 repeatability testing specifically to the AgileX PiPER, SO-101, or comparable sub-$200 leader-follower arms.** The closest analogue is the Kinova Gen3Lite (~$5,000), which exhibited substantial backlash-related positioning error around 2–6 mm (pqac-00000041). Low-cost arms with hobby servos and planetary gearboxes are expected to show similar or larger non-Gaussian error distributions due to backlash and compliance.

## 6. Software Tools Summary

| Tool/Library | Language | Key Capabilities for Accuracy Visualization | Published Reference | Availability/Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **pytransform3d** | Python | Represents uncertain SE(3) transforms with 6×6 covariance; composes globally and locally uncertain transforms with `concat_globally_uncertain_transforms` and `concat_locally_uncertain_transforms`; changes covariance frames with `adjoint_from_transform`; projects 6D confidence hyperellipsoids into 3D; supports trajectory covariance, URDF kinematics, Matplotlib, and Open3D. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000044) | Fabisch & Popescu, *Frontiers in Robotics and AI* (2026), [doi:10.3389/frobt.2026.1860457](https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2026.1860457) | Open-source Python library. Particularly suitable for an inexpensive, scriptable pipeline from URDF and measured covariance to ellipsoids along a trajectory. |
| **MATLAB + Unity3D Digital Twin** | MATLAB; C#/Unity | MATLAB performs Monte Carlo propagation, covariance/eigendecomposition, RMS and P95 calculations, and workspace sampling; Unity3D interactively renders color-coded probabilistic workspace point clouds, 3D error ellipsoids, and controller diagnostics. The published example used 10,000 trials at 50 configurations and a map of 3,000 configurations with 500 trials each. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000036) | Makhambetov et al., *Electronics* (2026), [doi:10.3390/electronics15143095](https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15143095) | MATLAB and Unity are separate products; Unity has free-use tiers, while MATLAB generally requires a license. The cited manipulator analysis is simulation-only, so its maps should not be treated as measured arm performance. |
| **RoboDK** | Python API; proprietary application | Robot simulation and offline programming; defines an ISO test cube and measurement plane, teaches targets on surfaces, generates point-visit programs, checks reachability, and visualizes nominal paths. Pollák and Goryl used it to prepare five ISO-style targets and separate X/Y measurement programs. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026) | Pollák & Goryl, *Machines* (2023), [doi:10.3390/machines11070734](https://doi.org/10.3390/machines11070734) | Commercial software with educational/trial options. The cited evidence does **not** establish a built-in statistical repeatability-map or covariance-ellipsoid facility; export measurements to Python or MATLAB for those analyses. |
| **Probabilistic Product-of-Exponentials (PPOE)** | Mathematical model; research implementations commonly in C++/Python/MATLAB | Lie-group-based probabilistic kinematics that represents correlated, configuration-dependent errors and propagates them along a kinematic chain to a 6-DoF end-effector covariance. Demonstrated on a Kinova Jaco2 with AprilTag observations and VICON ground truth; suitable for configuration-dependent covariance or projected confidence-volume displays. (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000042) | Meyer, Strobl & Triebel, IROS (2022), [doi:10.1109/IROS47612.2022.9981399](https://doi.org/10.1109/IROS47612.2022.9981399) | A modeling method rather than a turnkey visualization application. A practical implementation path is PPOE covariance propagation followed by pytransform3d, Open3D, or RViz rendering. |
| **ROS / RViz** | C++; Python; ROS messages | ROS `tf`/`tf2` maintains frame relationships; RViz displays robot models, measured and commanded paths, point clouds, arrows, and custom marker or triangle meshes that can encode ellipsoids. It can serve as the live display layer for AprilTag-derived TCP samples and path-error overlays. pytransform3d’s `TransformManager` is explicitly inspired by ROS `tf`. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009) | No dedicated peer-reviewed accuracy-map implementation was established in the retrieved evidence; related transformation and uncertainty functionality is documented by Fabisch & Popescu (2026), [doi:10.3389/frobt.2026.1860457](https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2026.1860457) | Open source and well suited to live experiments. Ellipsoid fitting, confidence scaling, and repeatability statistics must be calculated in a separate node; RViz primarily renders the resulting markers. |
| **MATLAB Robotics Toolbox / NumPy + SciPy** | MATLAB or Python | General-purpose implementation route for forward kinematics, Jacobians, covariance estimation, eigendecomposition, Monte Carlo sampling, RMS/P95 statistics, interpolation, and ellipsoid meshes. The core operations are Σₓ = JΣqJᵀ and Σ = VDVᵀ, with confidence semi-axes derived from √λ. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000030) | The retrieved literature supports the underlying workflow in Makhambetov et al. (2026), [doi:10.3390/electronics15143095](https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15143095), and Issametova et al. (2026), [doi:10.3390/math14030580](https://doi.org/10.3390/math14030580) | NumPy/SciPy are open source; MATLAB and some toolboxes require licenses. No retrieved paper establishes a one-click repeatability-map function in either stack—the analysis must be assembled from their numerical and plotting primitives. |


*Table: Software and computational frameworks for turning measured or modeled robot-position errors into ellipsoids, workspace maps, and trajectory-error displays. The notes distinguish turnkey visualization features from tools that require custom statistical processing.*

## 7. Practical Recommendations for Low-Cost Arms

For the user's AgileX PiPER and SO-101 arms with AprilTag-based measurement:

1. **Collect repeated TCP measurements** at ≥5 workspace locations following the ISO 9283 protocol (30 cycles per location, unidirectional approach). AprilTags detected by the fixed cameras provide the external position reference. Record raw 3D coordinates.

2. **Compute error ellipsoids** at each location using NumPy: subtract the mean, form the 3×3 covariance matrix, and eigendecompose. Plot 3σ ellipsoids using Matplotlib or Open3D. The eigenvalues reveal whether error is isotropic or dominated by a particular direction (e.g., gravity-axis compliance).

3. **Build a workspace map** by repeating step 1 across a grid of reachable locations. Color-code each point by its RMS repeatability and render as a 3D scatter plot. This requires no laser tracker and can be performed with the existing camera infrastructure.

4. **Use pytransform3d** for Jacobian-based propagation if a URDF model of the arm is available. The `concat_locally_uncertain_transforms` function propagates joint-angle covariances through the kinematic chain, and the projected hyperellipsoid visualization shows the resulting end-effector uncertainty (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011).

5. **Plot path error** by commanding a straight-line or circular trajectory, recording the measured TCP path at high frequency, and computing cross-track and along-track deviations as a function of path parameter. ISO 9283 path repeatability compares the envelope of deviations across multiple traversals (pqac-00000020).

## 8. Gaps in Published Evidence

- No peer-reviewed study applies error ellipsoid or probabilistic workspace mapping to the AgileX PiPER, SO-101, or comparable sub-$200 robot arms.
- No published software provides a turnkey, one-click repeatability map function; assembly from numerical primitives is required (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000019).
- The Makhambetov et al. (2026) workspace maps and error ellipsoids are simulation-only and have not been validated against physical measurements (pqac-00000019).
- Path-error visualization (error plotted continuously along a trajectory rather than at discrete points) is described mathematically but not demonstrated with dedicated software in the retrieved literature (pqac-00000002).
- The Sinha and Chakraborty (2019) robust IK work with error ellipsoids is a preprint (DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.1910.10852) and has not appeared in a peer-reviewed venue (pqac-00000030).
- The Franzese et al. (2025) MUKCa calibration study for Franka, KUKA, and Kinova is a preprint (DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2503.12584) (pqac-00000041).

Measurements were obtained from repeated image acquisitions of ArUco markers or markerless blob analysis. contexts.context: The excerpt describes a probabilistic, Jacobian-based approach for visualizing robot positioning accuracy and repeatability in 3D. Robot parameter or drive-error uncertainties are represented by a covariance matrix Σq and propagated through the kinematic Jacobian, using the relationship ΣX = JqΣqJqT. The resulting Cartesian covariance can be visualized as 3D error ellipsoids, whose size and orientation reflect positioning uncertainty. Applying this calculation throughout sampled joint configurations or workspace points produces a geometric reliability or repeatability map: central, compact configurations generally show higher reliability, while peripheral regions show lower reliability because Jacobian coefficients and sensitivity to parameter errors increase. Reliability is defined probabilistically as R = P(X ∈ Ω), where Ω is the acceptable positioning tolerance region. For trajectory analysis, the same calculation is evaluated along θ(t), allowing reliability, variance, or error to be plotted against path position or time; trajectory planners can constrain R(θ(t)) to remain above a required threshold. The excerpt does not identify a dedicated visualization software package. It mentions compatibility with modern FANUC control systems and recommends using reliability maps for workspace screening, configuration selection, trajectory optimization, and recalibration triggering. The framework is also extensible to mobile, redundant, parallel, and collaborative robots when their kinematics and uncertainty models are available.

Positioning-error distributions are approximately multivariate normal in compact and medium configurations, where covariance estimates agree with direct linearization. contexts.context: The excerpt documents pytransform3d’s tools for propagating and visualizing uncertainty in robot-arm transformations, but it does not discuss RoboDK or the MATLAB Robotics Toolbox. pytransform3d implements uncertainty propagation for SE(3) poses, including composition of uncertain transformations in a global reference frame through concat_globally_uncertain_transforms(A2B, cov_A2B, B2C, cov_B2C). contexts.context: The excerpt describes a stochastic ellipsoid and workspace-mapping procedure for robot positioning uncertainty. For a selected robot configuration, the position-error covariance matrix is decomposed into eigenvalues and eigenvectors. The eigenvectors define the principal directions of uncertainty, while the eigenvalues determine the ellipsoid semi-axis lengths; the displayed 3σ ellipsoid represents the corresponding uncertainty region and approximately 99.7% of realizations under the assumed distribution. Repeatability can therefore be characterized probabilistically by the ellipsoid’s orientation, axes, and volume, supplemented by sampled error vectors and RMS error. For probabilistic workspace maps, the method randomly samples thousands of end-effector or workspace configurations. At each configuration, Monte Carlo trials propagate modeled noise and uncertainty through the manipulator, producing position-error realizations, covariance estimates, RMS errors, and related statistics. The resulting Cartesian locations are rendered as a colored point cloud: green denotes RMS error below 5 mm, yellow 5–15 mm, and red above 15 mm. The excerpt reports 3000 workspace points with 500 Monte Carlo trials for visualization, while broader stochastic analysis uses 10,000 trials across 50 configurations. This approach reveals spatial accuracy regions and supports comparison between offline stochastic analysis and an interactive digital twin.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the covariance-based foundation for stochastic robot positioning. Kinematic and joint errors are modeled as random variables, typically with a multivariate normal distribution q ~ N(μq, Σq), where Σq can include correlations between parameters. Forward kinematics is linearized around the nominal or mean parameter vector: δX ≈ Jqδq. The end-effector pose covariance is then computed by propagating parameter covariance through the kinematic Jacobian: ΣX = JqΣqJqᵀ. An error ellipsoid for position is obtained from the relevant 3×3 translational block of ΣX: its principal axes and directions come from eigenvectors and eigenvalues, while a selected confidence level scales the semi-axis lengths by the corresponding chi-square quantile. For full pose uncertainty, a six-dimensional covariance can similarly describe position and orientation jointly, though orientation requires suitable angular treatment. A stochastic ellipsoid repeatability method therefore samples or propagates uncertain parameters, computes the resulting pose covariance, and represents repeatability with confidence ellipsoids. The excerpt does not describe a Monte Carlo workspace-map algorithm explicitly. However, Monte Carlo mapping would repeatedly draw q from N(μq, Σq), evaluate forward kinematics X = f(q) at workspace configurations, and aggregate empirical means, covariances, confidence ellipsoids, failure probabilities, or dispersion values into a spatial probabilistic/error map. High Jacobian conditioning and singular configurations produce larger mapped uncertainties.

contexts.context: The stochastic ellipsoid method represents robot positioning or repeatability uncertainty at each nominal configuration using the covariance of Monte Carlo end-effector errors. For every sampled joint configuration, the nominal position is computed, random joint and geometric perturbations are generated from the specified noise models, and each perturbed position is propagated through forward kinematics. The displacement samples are calculated as Δp = p_noisy − p_nom, then their covariance matrix Σ is eigendecomposed as Σ = VDVᵀ. The eigenvectors in V define the principal directions of the uncertainty ellipsoid, while the eigenvalues λj represent variances along those directions. A 3σ ellipsoid uses semi-axis lengths aj = 3√λj; its volume, (4/3)π∏aj, summarizes total three-dimensional uncertainty while retaining directional information that scalar RMS omits. Monte Carlo workspace maps repeat this process across many configurations. The excerpt describes 50 configurations with 10,000 noise trials each for detailed analysis, and a separate workspace probability map using 3,000 uniformly sampled configurations within joint limits and 500 trials per point, totaling 1,500,000 forward-kinematics evaluations. RMS and P95 errors provide scalar accuracy measures, while ellipsoid parameters and spatial aggregation characterize probabilistic accuracy throughout the reachable workspace.

contexts.context: The excerpt establishes the methodological basis for stochastic robot-positioning analysis but does not provide the explicit formulas for covariance-based error ellipsoids or detailed workspace-map construction. The robot is first modeled deterministically using Denavit–Hartenberg transformations and the direct-kinematics matrix. The Jacobian then propagates small joint deviations into end-effector pose deviations according to δx ≈ J(θ)δθ. In a stochastic extension, kinematic parameters and control variables are treated as random variables with specified distributions, producing a distribution of end-effector posture. This framework is the foundation for computing covariance propagation and, consequently, error ellipsoids: joint-space covariance would ordinarily be mapped into task space through the Jacobian, typically as Σx ≈ JΣθJᵀ, with ellipsoid axes and sizes determined from the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of Σx. For robot repeatability, the excerpt describes geometric reliability as the probability that the stochastic end-effector pose remains within permissible technological limits. Analytical probability estimates are used for simple domains, while Monte Carlo simulation handles nonlinearities and complex tolerances. Repeated random sampling of the uncertain parameters, forward-kinematics evaluation, and classification of samples against spatial or pose requirements can therefore generate probabilistic workspace or error maps. The study’s workflow also includes experimental and numerical validation.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports a covariance-based and simulation-based treatment of robot positioning uncertainty, although it does not provide the explicit mathematical construction of an error ellipsoid or a formal definition of the stochastic ellipsoid method. It reports that analytical models agree well with Monte Carlo results in compact and medium configurations, where positioning errors are close to normal and covariance structures match direct linear approximations. In such cases, covariance matrices can therefore characterize the error distribution and its principal directions and variances. For elongated configurations, nonlinear forward kinematics produce asymmetric and shifted error distributions; experimental ellipsoids differed from model predictions, with major-axis displacement up to 10–11° and variance increases up to 20%. The authors consequently recommend Monte Carlo simulation and nonlinear corrections for precision applications. For workspace mapping, the study evaluates positioning reliability across workspace configurations and constructs a two-dimensional geometric reliability map. The map represents the probability of successful positioning, with approximately 0.70 reliability in low-reliability peripheral regions and approximately 0.98 in high-reliability central regions. The central workspace corresponds to compact configurations, while reliability decreases toward workspace boundaries.

contexts.context: The excerpt illustrates a stochastic ellipsoid and probabilistic workspace-map workflow for robot positioning. At selected workspace locations, repeated Monte Carlo error samples are generated under combined noise conditions, and 3σ error ellipsoids are used to represent the resulting positional uncertainty. In the conventional covariance-based construction, the ellipsoid is centered at the nominal end-effector position and its principal directions are the eigenvectors of the Cartesian position covariance matrix; the semi-axis lengths are proportional to the square roots of the corresponding eigenvalues, with the multiplier set to the desired confidence level (such as 3σ). The reported ellipsoids are anisotropic: their longest axis is primarily vertical, consistent with gravity-induced elastic deformation. Their volumes and aspect ratios vary by workspace region, providing repeatability and tolerance information. The stochastic ellipsoid method therefore captures not only overall variance but also directional and configuration-dependent uncertainty. For probabilistic workspace maps, the study samples 3,000 robot configurations and performs 500 Monte Carlo trials per configuration, totaling 1,500,000 evaluations. Error statistics are then aggregated at each configuration, including RMS positioning error and the 95th-percentile error, and plotted spatially using color maps. The maps reveal low-error central regions and higher errors at elevated, extended-arm configurations.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a stochastic error-ellipsoid approach for robot positioning and repeatability. Positioning uncertainty is represented as a spatial distribution of end-effector errors; its covariance determines the ellipsoid’s principal directions and spread. The ellipsoid axes align with directions of greatest variability, which are associated with large sensitivities in the Jacobian (Jacobi) matrix. Nearly spherical ellipsoids indicate similar sensitivity in all directions, while elongated or inclined ellipsoids indicate anisotropic uncertainty and correlated link or drive errors. The study compares compact, medium, and elongated robot configurations. For the FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L, measurements used 25 workspace points and 50 repeated trials per point, with a laser tracker accurate to about 0.01 mm. These repeated samples were used to construct empirical error distributions and covariance matrices, which were compared against model predictions. Monte Carlo analysis was especially important in highly nonlinear or elongated configurations, where analytical and stochastic estimates differed by 7–10%; compact and medium configurations differed by only 1–3%. Thus, probabilistic workspace mapping involves sampling model uncertainties across configurations, estimating covariance/error ellipsoids at workspace locations, and using the resulting map to identify sensitive regions and optimize configurations before assembly or during online condition assessment.
contexts.question: How are error ellipsoids computed from covariance matrices in robot positioning? What is the stochastic ellipsoid method for robot repeatability? How is Monte Carlo simulation used to create workspace error maps or probabilistic workspace maps for robot arms?

contexts.context: ISO 9283 provides 14 robot-performance tests. Testing is conducted at maximum possible payload and speed, using an imaginary ISO cube positioned in the robot workspace. A selected diagonal and measurement points are used; the example selects five points, P1–P5, and the position-accuracy protocol requires 100% payload, 100% speed, five measuring points, and 30 cycles. Position accuracy (AP) is the deviation between the commanded position and the mean achieved position. The excerpt identifies unidirectional position repeatability (RP), path repeatability (RT), distance accuracy (AD), and distance repeatability (RD) as related criteria, although complete repeatability-specific trial conditions are not shown. ISO 9283 does not prescribe a particular metrology system. Reported tools and results include a laser tracker, laser interferometer, and Renishaw ballbar used on an ABB IRB 1600: repeatability was 22–37 mm with the laser tracker, 6–14 mm with the laser interferometer, and circularity deviation was below 1 mm with the ballbar. Other tested arms include a Yaskawa Motoman HP20F, whose repeatability worsened with increasing cycles and was several hundredths of a millimeter worse than its stated RP = 0.06 mm, and an ABB IRB 1200 5/0.9, whose thermal-drift repeatability improved from about 200 µm to 25 µm after compensation. The excerpt also mentions an ABB IRB 120 calibrated using FARO and C-Track systems, reducing position error by nearly 5 mm.

It describes an in-situ robot-remastering experiment using a 7-degree-of-freedom KUKA arm operated in high-stiffness joint-position control. The laser tracker served as a benchmark reference, while the motion-capture system provided the unconventional lower-cost reference measurement system; two systems were used for benchmarking and validation, although only one would be required in practice. The excerpt’s figure references Vernier scales on both KUKA and Fanuc arms, but the described experimental system and reported remastering result concern the KUKA arm. Visual remastering produced average Cartesian positioning errors of several millimeters, with extreme errors up to 10 mm. contexts.context: The excerpt provides the clearest ISO 9283 protocol for the CRS A255 experiment, but it does not reproduce the full standard’s positioning-accuracy procedure or a separate accuracy success threshold. The CRS A255 is a 5-DOF robot with a specified repeatability of 0.05 mm, a 2 kg maximum payload, and a maximum speed of 0.508 m/s. Position was measured using a three-dimensional system of dial gauges equipped with capacitive Sylvac instruments, with 0.005 mm measurement accuracy; orientation was excluded because the system measured only linear position. Experiments used 15 target locations distributed across three heights, with the end effector entering the measurement system at 45 degrees. In accordance with ISO 9283, each test comprised 30 cycles and was repeated 30 times, producing 900 measurements per target location. Repeatability was calculated from the average 3D positional deviation and the standard deviation of that deviation. Statistical significance was assessed with Friedman’s nonparametric test for location differences and t-tests for identical locations at different heights. The study found statistically significant repeatability differences among target locations, relative positions, locations at the same height, and the same location at different heights. Its error model agreed with experimental results, and repeatability generally worsened as targets became farther from the robot. The excerpt also reports a Baxter-related speed/payload study: slower speeds and lighter payloads generally improved repeatability, but speed and payload interacted and could not be evaluated independently.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes an ISO 9283-oriented contact measurement procedure for a welding robot. An ISO cube with a 1200 mm edge was positioned in the robot’s most frequently used welding area. Five points, P1–P5, were measured on a selected plane, while the Z-axis was omitted because the robot’s touch-sensing function determines workpiece distance in that direction. The study used two measurement protocols. Phase 1 was contact-based: a custom 20 mm-radius spherical end-effector, a 20 × 20 × 20 mm calibration cube, and a three-axis mechanical dial-indicator fixture measured displacement along X, Y, and Z. Phase 2 was non-contact and used a calibrated OptiTrack multi-camera vision system. Its first sub-phase replicated the P1–P2 motion, while the second assessed repeatability at five positions forming an ISO 9283 virtual cube. A 4 kg payload was attached during the vision trials. Motion Perfect controlled programming, RoboDK supported simulation, and MATLAB handled filtering, geometric-center calculations, and statistical evaluation. snippets: This thesis applies the ISO 9283 framework to assess the repeatability performance of the RTA ARTIC6-1215-6kg industrial robot.
The robot was programmed to move repeatedly between two Cartesian positions, P1 and P2, performing 30 motion cycles.
The positional deviation at each endpoint was recorded and used as the basis for statistical analysis of contact-based repeatability.
The first phase employed a mechanical contact-based setup.
Repeatability measurements were collected using a three-axis mechanical dial indicator fixture, with indicators arranged orthogonally to measure displacement along the X, Y, and Z directions.
The second phase introduced a non-contact measurement strategy using a calibrated multi-camera vision setup.
the second evaluated the robot's repeatability at five distinct positions forming a virtual cube in space, consistent with the ISO 9283 “ISO cube” configuration.
To reflect realistic industrial conditions, a 4 kg payload was mounted on the end-effector during the vision-based trials.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents a repeatable 3D pose-accuracy protocol using a Kinova Jaco2 on the LRU: AprilTags on the end-effector provide 2D camera bearings, while a grasped VICON target supplies ground truth. contexts.context: The 2019 ASME paper models joint uncertainty as a ball, \(\delta\Theta^T\delta\Theta\le c=(k\sigma)^2\), or Gaussian \(\delta\Theta\sim N(0,\sigma^2I)\), then linearizes forward kinematics: \(\delta X\approx J_p\delta\Theta\). It derives the 3D positional error ellipsoid \(\delta X^T(J_pJ_p^T)^{-1}\delta X\le c\), explicitly stating, “Equation (5) describes the set of position errors… Geometrically, the set…is an ellipsoid.” Orientation is similarly propagated via quaternion Jacobians. This is a parameter-based worst-case/probabilistic visualization method, not a measured repeatability protocol; no arm, trials, software, DOI, or empirical validation appears in the excerpt.

contexts.context: Makhambetov et al. (Electronics, 2026; DOI: “10.3390/electronics15143095”) presents a **simulation-only** method, not a physical-arm benchmark. It models encoder noise, thermal drift, elastic deformation, and geometric tolerances, propagating them through kinematics with **10,000 Monte Carlo trials across 50 configurations**; **3,000 sampled configurations** produce probabilistic workspace maps and **3D error ellipsoids**. Elastic deformation contributed **99.97%** of RMS uncertainty and was **45.94×** encoder noise. Unity3D visualizes maps and ellipsoids. The paper states: “without requiring physical hardware,” so it provides no measured repeatability, arm-specific validation, or protocol for PiPER/SO-101.

Validation used an equivalent slide-link tribometer, not a named robot: steel 42CD4 plate and 100C6 pin, room temperature, 0.1–3 m/s sliding speed, 40–150 N load, with friction measured by strain gauge and coefficient \(f=F/N\). contexts.context: The excerpt reports results only for the FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L; it provides no information about Kinova, UR5, Franka, ABB, or other low-cost robot arms. For the FANUC arm, analytical and Monte Carlo models agreed closely in compact and medium configurations, where errors were approximately normal and covariance estimates matched direct linearization. In the elongated configuration, nonlinear kinematic effects caused asymmetric and shifted error distributions. Experimental error ellipsoids showed that the major axis could be displaced by up to 10–11° relative to model predictions, with variance up to 20% higher than predicted. The study also constructed a workspace geometric-reliability map representing successful positioning probability. Reliability was approximately 0.98 in central workspace regions associated with compact configurations and declined toward the workspace boundaries, reaching low values around 0.70 in peripheral zones. The excerpt additionally reports that positioning accuracy degraded over time: average position error increased from 0.018 mm in the first three months to 0.041 mm in the last three months, while average orientation error rose from 0.28° to 0.71°. Thus, the provided passage supports detailed conclusions for FANUC only, not comparative results for the other named robot families.

contexts.context: The excerpt evaluates a single robot arm and does not identify its manufacturer or model. Consequently, it provides no model-specific results for Kinova, FANUC, UR5, Franka, ABB, or other explicitly named low-cost arms, nor does it compare error ellipsoids or workspace accuracy maps across those platforms. The reported analysis concerns theoretical absolute positioning error over 1,000 randomly generated joint configurations. Vernier remastering produced mean errors of approximately 6.1 mm (motion capture) and 5.6 mm (laser tracker) when zero-offset uncertainty alone was considered, while Bayesian remastering reduced these values to 0.223 mm and 0.183 mm, respectively. When zero-offset uncertainty, unmodeled dynamics, and noise were included, Bayesian remastering yielded mean errors of 1.439 mm and 1.187 mm, with upper-percentile errors below 3 mm. The authors concluded that accuracy improved by at least four-fold across the full workspace. They also found that zero-offset uncertainty accounted for more than 95% of the original Cartesian error after Vernier remastering, but only about 15% of the remaining error after Bayesian remastering.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports probabilistic positioning and reliability analysis only for the six-axis FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L; it does not mention Kinova, UR5, Franka, ABB, or low-cost robot arms, nor does it provide comparative results for those models using error ellipsoids or workspace-accuracy maps. For FANUC, Monte Carlo simulations incorporated stochastic DH-parameter and joint errors, nonlinear direct kinematics, complex permissible regions, correlated errors, and dependence on configuration and trajectory. The analysis produced a reliability map over joint-configuration space, allowing identification of more reliable postures and avoidance of singularity-prone regions. Independent errors in joints 4–6 were associated primarily with orientation errors, while correlated errors in joints 1–3 caused vertical or horizontal displacement of the working point. Correlated errors in DH parameters altered the spatial distribution of posture errors. The robot’s outstretched-arm configurations, particularly those with a large second-joint angle, showed significantly reduced reliability because of increased Jacobian sensitivity. The excerpt also notes that the robot has low independent drive errors, although thermal expansion can produce correlated errors. Monte Carlo was considered useful for complex configuration-dependent reliability assessment, despite high computational cost and the need for importance sampling in rare-event, low-reliability cases.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports experiments involving two robot platforms. First, it evaluates a simulated David humanoid robot, using fingertip contact with a simulated table to study residual end-effector pose errors. The PPOE covariance model encodes correlations between positional state variables and improves translational pose estimation; rotational error is largely unaffected. Second, it evaluates a planetary rover prototype (LRU) equipped with a Kinova Jaco2 arm. The arm’s end-effector pose is corrected by fusing 2D AprilTag image measurements with the 6D kinematic pose. The study models uncertainty from a flexing carbon-fiber base plate, joint errors, and hand-eye calibration residuals. In two experiments, PPOE-based 2D estimation achieved mean lateral errors of 0.29 ± 0.15 cm and 0.50 ± 0.25 cm, compared with 0.44 ± 0.29 cm and 0.52 ± 0.24 cm for a static naive covariance; forward kinematics alone produced 0.82 ± 0.49 cm and 1.48 ± 0.38 cm. (Lower priority) Visualizing repeatability: What methods and software show a robot's positioning accuracy and repeatability in 3D (error ellipsoids, repeatability maps, error along a path), computed from measurements or robot parameters?

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. For each benchmark or result, describe the protocol in enough detail to repeat it (what is measured, number of trials, success criterion, measuring tool) and give the arm model. # Visualizing Robot Positioning Accuracy and Repeatability in 3D

## 1. Overview

Three principal methods appear in the published literature for showing a robot's positioning accuracy and repeatability in three dimensions: **(1) error ellipsoids** (the stochastic ellipsoid method), **(2) probabilistic workspace maps**, and **(3) Jacobian-based confidence volumes along a path or trajectory**. Each can be computed from physical measurements, from modeled parameter uncertainties, or from both. The table below summarizes these methods, their mathematical basis, published protocols, and supporting software.

| Method | What is Visualized | Mathematical Basis | Protocol Detail | Software/Tools | Key Reference (with DOI) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Error ellipsoids (stochastic ellipsoid method)** | A 3D confidence region around the nominal or mean TCP position. Orientation shows principal error directions, semi-axis lengths show directional dispersion, and volume summarizes overall uncertainty. | From measured or simulated Cartesian errors, compute covariance Σ and eigendecompose it as Σ = VDVᵀ. Eigenvectors give principal directions and eigenvalues λ_j give variances. A 3σ ellipsoid has semi-axes a_j = 3√λ_j. Joint-space uncertainty can also be propagated into task space through the Jacobian. (makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 5-7, issametova2026reliabilityinrobotics pages 13-15, sinha2019computingrobustinverse pages 3-4) | **Measured:** command the same pose repeatedly, record 3D TCP coordinates, subtract their mean, and estimate Σ. Issametova et al. tested a FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L at 25 workspace points with 50 trials per point using a laser tracker accurate to about 0.01 mm. **Modeled:** Makhambetov et al. used 10,000 Monte Carlo trials at each of 50 configurations; that study was simulation-only and deferred physical validation. (makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 5-7, issametova2026reliabilityinrobotics pages 37-39, makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 16-17) | NumPy/SciPy or MATLAB for covariance and eigendecomposition; Matplotlib, Plotly, Open3D, or Unity3D for rendering. The cited digital twin used MATLAB and Unity3D. | Makhambetov et al. (2026), [DOI 10.3390/electronics15143095](https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15143095); Issametova et al. (2026), [DOI 10.3390/math14030580](https://doi.org/10.3390/math14030580); Rezala and Arbaoui (2022), [DOI 10.5829/ije.2022.35.02b.21](https://doi.org/10.5829/ije.2022.35.02b.21); Sinha and Chakraborty (**preprint**, 2019), [DOI 10.48550/arXiv.1910.10852](https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.1910.10852). (makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 5-7, issametova2026reliabilityinrobotics pages 37-39, sinha2019computingrobustinverse pages 3-4, rezala2022analysisrandoncauses pages 2-4) |
| **Probabilistic workspace maps (Monte Carlo or repeated measurements)** | A color-coded 3D point cloud, voxel map, or sliced heat map over the reachable workspace. Each location can encode RMS error, P95 error, ellipsoid volume, ISO repeatability, or probability of remaining inside a task tolerance. | At each workspace location, generate or measure an error distribution and calculate RMS, P95, covariance, or reliability R = P(X ∈ Ω). Display measured samples directly or interpolate them only when spatial sampling is sufficiently dense. (issametova2026reliabilityinrobotics pages 48-49, makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 9-11, makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 11-14) | Makhambetov et al. sampled **3,000 configurations with 500 trials each**, totaling 1.5 million forward-kinematics evaluations. Points were green below 5 mm RMS, yellow from 5–15 mm, and red above 15 mm. Issametova et al. mapped successful-positioning probability for a FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L, reporting about 0.98 centrally and 0.70 near peripheral configurations. A hardware alternative is to repeat an ISO-style pose test across a grid of reachable points. (makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 9-11, issametova2026reliabilityinrobotics pages 45-48) | MATLAB or Python for Monte Carlo; Plotly, Open3D, or PyVista for point clouds and slices; Unity3D for an interactive digital twin. RoboDK can generate nominal configurations, but the cited evidence does not establish a built-in statistical repeatability-map function. | Makhambetov et al. (2026), [DOI 10.3390/electronics15143095](https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15143095); Issametova et al. (2026), [DOI 10.3390/math14030580](https://doi.org/10.3390/math14030580).
