## 2. Error Ellipsoids (Stochastic Ellipsoid Method)

### 2.1 Mathematical Construction

The stochastic ellipsoid method represents positioning uncertainty at a given robot configuration as a three-dimensional confidence region derived from the covariance of end-effector position errors. Makhambetov et al. describe the procedure: "The displacement samples are calculated as Δp = p_noisy − p_nom, then their covariance matrix Σ is eigendecomposed as Σ = VDVᵀ. The eigenvectors in V define the principal directions of the uncertainty ellipsoid, while the eigenvalues λ_j represent variances along those directions. A 3σ ellipsoid uses semi-axis lengths a_j = 3√λ_j" (makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 5-7). The volume of this ellipsoid, (4/3)π∏a_j, provides a scalar summary of total uncertainty while retaining directional information that a single RMS number discards (makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 5-7).

Alternatively, the ellipsoid can be computed analytically from the kinematic Jacobian. Issametova et al. explain: "Robot parameter or drive-error uncertainties are represented by a covariance matrix Σ_q and propagated through the kinematic Jacobian, using the relationship Σ_X = J_q Σ_q J_qᵀ" (issametova2026reliabilityinrobotics pages 48-49). The 3×3 translational block of Σ_X is then eigendecomposed to obtain the ellipsoid. For task-space error, Sinha and Chakraborty (preprint) show that joint-space uncertainty propagated through the position Jacobian J_p yields "δXᵀ(J_p J_pᵀ)⁻¹δX ≤ c," which "geometrically describes an ellipsoid" of position errors at the end-effector (sinha2019computingrobustinverse pages 3-4).

### 2.2 Protocol and Validation

Issametova et al. validated the ellipsoid approach experimentally on a **FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L**, measuring at "25 workspace points and 50 repeated trials per point, with a laser tracker accurate to about 0.01 mm" (issametova2026reliabilityinrobotics pages 37-39). They found that analytical and Monte Carlo ellipsoids agreed within 1–3% for compact and medium configurations, but diverged by 7–10% for elongated configurations where nonlinear kinematics dominate: "Experimental error ellipsoids showed that the major axis could be displaced by up to 10–11° relative to model predictions, with variance up to 20% higher than predicted" (issametova2026reliabilityinrobotics pages 45-48). This is a peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.3390/math14030580).

Makhambetov et al. used a purely computational approach on a generic 6-DOF manipulator with "N = 10,000 trials across 50 workspace configurations" and rendered 3σ error ellipsoids through a Unity3D Digital Twin (makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 1-2). Their ellipsoids were anisotropic, with the longest axis primarily vertical due to gravitational elastic deformation (makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 11-14). This is a peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.3390/electronics15143095) but contains no physical measurement validation; the authors note that "future work will compare them with measured end-effector scatter using a laser tracker" (makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 16-17).

Rezala and Arbaoui used the stochastic ellipsoid method to analyze repeatability errors caused by joint friction variations, noting that "the stochastic ellipsoid method is able to generate repeatability predictions for the entire workspace" (rezala2022analysisrandoncauses pages 2-4). This is a peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.5829/ije.2022.35.02b.21).

### 2.3 How to Repeat for Low-Cost Arms

For the AgileX PiPER or SO-101, one can command the arm to the same pose repeatedly (≥30 cycles per ISO 9283), record the TCP position using an AprilTag-based external camera system or a dial indicator, compute the 3×3 position covariance from the scatter, and eigendecompose it to obtain the ellipsoid axes and semi-lengths. This requires no laser tracker; the user's existing fixed cameras and AprilTags can serve as the measurement system, though with lower absolute accuracy than a laser tracker. **No published study has applied error ellipsoid analysis specifically to AgileX PiPER, SO-101, or comparable sub-$2,000 arms.**

## 3. Probabilistic Workspace Maps

### 3.1 Monte Carlo Workspace Characterization

Workspace maps extend single-point ellipsoid analysis to the entire reachable space. Makhambetov et al. constructed a "probabilistic workspace map using 3,000 uniformly sampled configurations within joint limits and 500 trials per point, totaling 1,500,000 forward-kinematics evaluations" (makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 5-7). The result is a color-coded 3D point cloud: "green denotes RMS error below 5 mm, yellow 5–15 mm, and red above 15 mm" (makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 9-11). The maps reveal that "central workspace corresponds to compact configurations" with low error, while "reliability decreases toward workspace boundaries" (issametova2026reliabilityinrobotics pages 45-48).

Issametova et al. constructed a geometric-reliability map for the FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L, defining reliability as the probability that the end-effector lands within a tolerance region. They report "approximately 0.98 in central workspace regions associated with compact configurations" declining to "approximately 0.70 in peripheral zones" (issametova2026reliabilityinrobotics pages 45-48). This was computed from both analytical (Jacobian-based) and Monte Carlo methods, peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.3390/math14030580).

### 3.2 Measurement-Based Workspace Maps

Chen applied the ISO 9283 protocol to the **Baxter** robot to generate "a 3D mapping of repeatability at different heights," finding that "repeatability generally deteriorated as the target moved farther from the robot" (chen2015applicationofthe pages 14-18). The protocol tested 15 target locations at three heights, with 30 cycles per experiment repeated 30 times (900 measurements per location), using 3D dial gauges with 0.005 mm accuracy (chen2015applicationofthea pages 14-18, chen2015applicationofthe pages 14-18). This is a thesis (2015).

### 3.3 ISO 9283 Protocol Summary

The ISO 9283 standard prescribes the canonical measurement protocol. A test cube is placed in the most-used workspace region with edges parallel to the robot base coordinates. Five poses (P1–P5) lie on a diagonal test plane, P1 at the cube center and P2–P5 near diagonal corners. The robot visits these poses in unidirectional order through 30 cycles at each of three speeds (10%, 50%, 100% of rated velocity) and 100% rated payload. Position repeatability is computed as "RP_l = mean distance from the barycentre plus three standard deviations" (chen2015applicationofthe pages 18-23, chen2015applicationofthea pages 18-23). This protocol has been applied with various measurement tools including laser trackers (Faro Vantage, accuracy ±0.009 mm), contact gauges, and vision systems (pollak2023simulationdesignand pages 2-4, płaczek2018testingofan pages 3-5).

## 4. Jacobian-Based Confidence Volumes and Error Along a Path

### 4.1 The Probabilistic Product-of-Exponentials (PPOE) Model

Meyer et al. presented the PPOE model at IROS 2022, which "does not only consider the robot's deterministic geometry but additionally models time-varying and configuration-dependent errors in a probabilistic way" (meyer2022theprobabilisticrobot pages 1-2). The model propagates errors along the kinematic chain using Lie-group operations and computes their influence on the end-effector pose. It was validated on a **Kinova Jaco2** arm, where "PPOE-based 2D estimation achieved mean lateral errors of 0.29 ± 0.15 cm and 0.50 ± 0.25 cm" compared with forward kinematics alone at "0.82 ± 0.49 cm and 1.48 ± 0.38 cm" (meyer2022theprobabilisticrobot pages 6-8). This is a peer-reviewed IEEE conference paper (DOI: 10.1109/IROS47612.2022.9981399).

### 4.2 pytransform3d: An Open-Source Uncertainty Visualization Library

The Python library pytransform3d provides the most accessible implementation for low-cost arm users. Fabisch and Popescu describe its uncertainty module: it "models uncertain rigid transformations using a transformation-matrix mean and a 6×6 covariance matrix over exponential coordinates" and supports "composition, inversion, and fusion of uncertain transformations" (fabisch2026newfeaturesof pages 9-10). Key functions include `concat_locally_uncertain_transforms(A2B, B2C, cov_A, cov_B)` for propagating joint-displacement covariances, and `adjoint_from_transform(A2B)` for transferring covariance between frames (fabisch2026newfeaturesof pages 12-13). The library renders "an equiprobable projected 6D pose hyperellipsoid at configurable kσ intervals in 3D; the example describes a 3σ hyperellipsoid, corresponding to 99.7% probability" (fabisch2026newfeaturesof pages 9-10). Importantly, the authors note that "an ellipsoid is not an appropriate representation" for all cases because rotation-translation coupling can produce banana-shaped distributions rather than ordinary ellipsoids (fabisch2026newfeaturesof pages 10-12). The library supports URDF loading through `UrdfTransformManager` and visualization through both Matplotlib and Open3D (fabisch2026newfeaturesof pages 10-12, fabisch2026newfeaturesof pages 6-9). This is a peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.3389/frobt.2026.1860457).

### 4.3 Path-Error Visualization

For error along a path, Issametova et al. describe evaluating the Jacobian-based reliability calculation "along θ(t), allowing reliability, variance, or error to be plotted against path position or time; trajectory planners can constrain R(θ(t)) to remain above a required threshold" (issametova2026reliabilityinrobotics pages 48-49). ISO 9283 also defines path accuracy and path repeatability as separate criteria measured by recording the continuous trajectory and comparing it with the commanded path (pollak2023simulationdesignand pages 2-4).

## 5. Calibration Context: Comparative Results Across Arm Models

While this review focuses on visualization rather than calibration, several papers provide comparative positioning-accuracy results that establish the baseline these visualizations would display:

- **FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L**: Positioning error increased from 0.018 mm (first 3 months) to 0.041 mm (last 3 months) in operational monitoring (issametova2026reliabilityinrobotics pages 45-48).
- **Kinova Jaco2**: Forward kinematics error of 0.82–1.48 cm, reduced to 0.29–0.50 cm with PPOE-based sensor fusion using AprilTags (meyer2022theprobabilisticrobot pages 6-8).
- **Franka Panda**: Mean absolute positioning error reduced from ~10 mm to 0.24–0.35 mm by MUKCa calibration; Kinova Gen3Lite improved from 5.99 mm to 2.66 mm, with remaining error attributed to "joint backlash in planetary gearboxes" (franzese2025mukcaaccurateand pages 4-6). This is a preprint (DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2503.12584).
- **Generic 7-DOF arm** (Wyk et al., preprint): Bayesian remastering using a motion capture system reduced "the average robot positioning error to 0.26 mm" and the "average absolute positioning error" from over 4 mm (Vernier method) to "within 1.5 mm" with Bayesian zero-offset optimization (wyk2019efficientlyimprovingand pages 3-4, wyk2019efficientlyimprovingand pages 7-8).
- **Kuka KR 16-2**: Tested per PN-EN 9283 with a Faro Vantage laser tracker (accuracy ±0.009 mm), 30 measurements per test configuration, robot warmed up with a 40-minute cycle (płaczek2018testingofan pages 3-5).
- **Panasonic TM-2000**: ISO 9283 contact-measurement protocol, 1200 mm ISO cube, 5 points, 30 cycles, 50% max speed, 3 kg load, ambient 20–22°C (pollak2023simulationdesignand pages 1-2, pollak2023simulationdesignand pages 7-9).

**No published study was found that applies error ellipsoid analysis, probabilistic workspace mapping, or ISO 9283 repeatability testing specifically to the AgileX PiPER, SO-101, or comparable sub-$200 leader-follower arms.** The closest analogue is the Kinova Gen3Lite (~$5,000), which exhibited substantial backlash-related positioning error around 2–6 mm (franzese2025mukcaaccurateand pages 4-6). Low-cost arms with hobby servos and planetary gearboxes are expected to show similar or larger non-Gaussian error distributions due to backlash and compliance.

## 7. Practical Recommendations for Low-Cost Arms

For the user's AgileX PiPER and SO-101 arms with AprilTag-based measurement:

1. **Collect repeated TCP measurements** at ≥5 workspace locations following the ISO 9283 protocol (30 cycles per location, unidirectional approach). AprilTags detected by the fixed cameras provide the external position reference. Record raw 3D coordinates.

2. **Compute error ellipsoids** at each location using NumPy: subtract the mean, form the 3×3 covariance matrix, and eigendecompose. Plot 3σ ellipsoids using Matplotlib or Open3D. The eigenvalues reveal whether error is isotropic or dominated by a particular direction (e.g., gravity-axis compliance).

3. **Build a workspace map** by repeating step 1 across a grid of reachable locations. Color-code each point by its RMS repeatability and render as a 3D scatter plot. This requires no laser tracker and can be performed with the existing camera infrastructure.

4. **Use pytransform3d** for Jacobian-based propagation if a URDF model of the arm is available. The `concat_locally_uncertain_transforms` function propagates joint-angle covariances through the kinematic chain, and the projected hyperellipsoid visualization shows the resulting end-effector uncertainty (fabisch2026newfeaturesof pages 9-10, fabisch2026newfeaturesof pages 12-13).

5. **Plot path error** by commanding a straight-line or circular trajectory, recording the measured TCP path at high frequency, and computing cross-track and along-track deviations as a function of path parameter. ISO 9283 path repeatability compares the envelope of deviations across multiple traversals (pollak2023simulationdesignand pages 2-4).

## 8. Gaps in Published Evidence

- No peer-reviewed study applies error ellipsoid or probabilistic workspace mapping to the AgileX PiPER, SO-101, or comparable sub-$200 robot arms.
- No published software provides a turnkey, one-click repeatability map function; assembly from numerical primitives is required (fabisch2026newfeaturesof pages 9-10, makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 16-17).
- The Makhambetov et al. (2026) workspace maps and error ellipsoids are simulation-only and have not been validated against physical measurements (makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 16-17).
- Path-error visualization (error plotted continuously along a trajectory rather than at discrete points) is described mathematically but not demonstrated with dedicated software in the retrieved literature (issametova2026reliabilityinrobotics pages 48-49).
- The Sinha and Chakraborty (2019) robust IK work with error ellipsoids is a preprint (DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.1910.10852) and has not appeared in a peer-reviewed venue (sinha2019computingrobustinverse pages 3-4).
- The Franzese et al. (2025) MUKCa calibration study for Franka, KUKA, and Kinova is a preprint (DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2503.12584) (franzese2025mukcaaccurateand pages 4-6).

| Method | What is Visualized | Mathematical Basis | Protocol Detail | Software/Tools | Key Reference (with DOI) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Error ellipsoids (stochastic ellipsoid method)** | A 3D confidence region around the nominal or mean TCP position. Orientation shows principal error directions, semi-axis lengths show directional dispersion, and volume summarizes overall uncertainty. | From measured or simulated Cartesian errors, compute covariance Σ and eigendecompose it as Σ = VDVᵀ. Eigenvectors give principal directions and eigenvalues λ_j give variances. A 3σ ellipsoid has semi-axes a_j = 3√λ_j. Joint-space uncertainty can also be propagated into task space through the Jacobian. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000030) | **Measured:** command the same pose repeatedly, record 3D TCP coordinates, subtract their mean, and estimate Σ. Issametova et al. tested a FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L at 25 workspace points with 50 trials per point using a laser tracker accurate to about 0.01 mm. **Modeled:** Makhambetov et al. used 10,000 Monte Carlo trials at each of 50 configurations; that study was simulation-only and deferred physical validation. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000019) | NumPy/SciPy or MATLAB for covariance and eigendecomposition; Matplotlib, Plotly, Open3D, or Unity3D for rendering. The cited digital twin used MATLAB and Unity3D. | Makhambetov et al. (2026), [DOI 10.3390/electronics15143095](https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15143095); Issametova et al. (2026), [DOI 10.3390/math14030580](https://doi.org/10.3390/math14030580); Rezala and Arbaoui (2022), [DOI 10.5829/ije.2022.35.02b.21](https://doi.org/10.5829/ije.2022.35.02b.21); Sinha and Chakraborty (**preprint**, 2019), [DOI 10.48550/arXiv.1910.10852](https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.1910.10852). (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000035) |
| **Probabilistic workspace maps (Monte Carlo or repeated measurements)** | A color-coded 3D point cloud, voxel map, or sliced heat map over the reachable workspace. Each location can encode RMS error, P95 error, ellipsoid volume, ISO repeatability, or probability of remaining inside a task tolerance. | At each workspace location, generate or measure an error distribution and calculate RMS, P95, covariance, or reliability R = P(X ∈ Ω). Display measured samples directly or interpolate them only when spatial sampling is sufficiently dense. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014) | Makhambetov et al. sampled **3,000 configurations with 500 trials each**, totaling 1.5 million forward-kinematics evaluations. Points were green below 5 mm RMS, yellow from 5–15 mm, and red above 15 mm. Issametova et al. mapped successful-positioning probability for a FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L, reporting about 0.98 centrally and 0.70 near peripheral configurations. A hardware alternative is to repeat an ISO-style pose test across a grid of reachable points. (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000039) | MATLAB or Python for Monte Carlo; Plotly, Open3D, or PyVista for point clouds and slices; Unity3D for an interactive digital twin. RoboDK can generate nominal configurations, but the cited evidence does not establish a built-in statistical repeatability-map function. | Makhambetov et al. (2026), [DOI 10.3390/electronics15143095](https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15143095); Issametova et al. (2026), [DOI 10.3390/math14030580](https://doi.org/10.3390/math14030580). (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000039) |
| **Jacobian-based propagation and confidence volumes along a path** | Configuration-dependent confidence volumes at sampled trajectory poses, plus plots of cross-track error, along-track error, orientation error, RMS, or tolerance probability versus time or arc length. Full SE(3) uncertainty may project into a curved or banana-shaped volume rather than a true Cartesian ellipsoid. | Linearized propagation uses δX ≈ J_qδq and Σ_X = J_qΣ_qJ_qᵀ. For measured paths, time-align commanded and measured poses, compute their relative transform, and resolve translation into tangent and normal components. A 6×6 SE(3) covariance can be transported between frames with the adjoint and projected into 3D. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000016) | Estimate Σ_q from stationary joint logs, encoder specifications, calibration residuals, or fitted parameter uncertainty. Evaluate the Jacobian and propagate covariance at every path sample, then validate with repeated externally measured runs. ISO 9283-style pose testing uses five poses on a diagonal plane and 30 cycles per speed/payload condition. Meyer et al. demonstrated configuration-dependent covariance on a Kinova Jaco2 using AprilTags and VICON ground truth at 9 and 29 configurations. (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000042) | **pytransform3d** supports SE(3) covariance composition, inversion, adjoint frame changes, URDF kinematics, and projected 6D confidence hyperellipsoids through Matplotlib or Open3D. ROS/tf and RViz can display frames, paths, markers, and custom ellipsoid meshes. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000044) | Fabisch and Popescu (2026), [DOI 10.3389/frobt.2026.1860457](https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2026.1860457); Meyer et al., IROS 2022, [DOI 10.1109/IROS47612.2022.9981399](https://doi.org/10.1109/iros47612.2022.9981399). (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029) |

artifacts.artifact-01:
| Tool/Library | Language | Key Capabilities for Accuracy Visualization | Published Reference | Availability/Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **pytransform3d** | Python | Represents uncertain SE(3) transforms with 6×6 covariance; composes globally and locally uncertain transforms with `concat_globally_uncertain_transforms` and `concat_locally_uncertain_transforms`; changes covariance frames with `adjoint_from_transform`; projects 6D confidence hyperellipsoids into 3D; supports trajectory covariance, URDF kinematics, Matplotlib, and Open3D. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000044) | Fabisch & Popescu, *Frontiers in Robotics and AI* (2026), [doi:10.3389/frobt.2026.1860457](https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2026.1860457) | Open-source Python library. Particularly suitable for an inexpensive, scriptable pipeline from URDF and measured covariance to ellipsoids along a trajectory. |
| **MATLAB + Unity3D Digital Twin** | MATLAB; C#/Unity | MATLAB performs Monte Carlo propagation, covariance/eigendecomposition, RMS and P95 calculations, and workspace sampling; Unity3D interactively renders color-coded probabilistic workspace point clouds, 3D error ellipsoids, and controller diagnostics. The published example used 10,000 trials at 50 configurations and a map of 3,000 configurations with 500 trials each. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000036) | Makhambetov et al., *Electronics* (2026), [doi:10.3390/electronics15143095](https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15143095) | MATLAB and Unity are separate products; Unity has free-use tiers, while MATLAB generally requires a license. The cited manipulator analysis is simulation-only, so its maps should not be treated as measured arm performance. |
| **RoboDK** | Python API; proprietary application | Robot simulation and offline programming; defines an ISO test cube and measurement plane, teaches targets on surfaces, generates point-visit programs, checks reachability, and visualizes nominal paths. Pollák and Goryl used it to prepare five ISO-style targets and separate X/Y measurement programs. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026) | Pollák & Goryl, *Machines* (2023), [doi:10.3390/machines11070734](https://doi.org/10.3390/machines11070734) | Commercial software with educational/trial options. The cited evidence does **not** establish a built-in statistical repeatability-map or covariance-ellipsoid facility; export measurements to Python or MATLAB for those analyses. |
| **Probabilistic Product-of-Exponentials (PPOE)** | Mathematical model; research implementations commonly in C++/Python/MATLAB | Lie-group-based probabilistic kinematics that represents correlated, configuration-dependent errors and propagates them along a kinematic chain to a 6-DoF end-effector covariance. Demonstrated on a Kinova Jaco2 with AprilTag observations and VICON ground truth; suitable for configuration-dependent covariance or projected confidence-volume displays. (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000042) | Meyer, Strobl & Triebel, IROS (2022), [doi:10.1109/IROS47612.2022.9981399](https://doi.org/10.1109/IROS47612.2022.9981399) | A modeling method rather than a turnkey visualization application. A practical implementation path is PPOE covariance propagation followed by pytransform3d, Open3D, or RViz rendering. |
| **ROS / RViz** | C++; Python; ROS messages | ROS `tf`/`tf2` maintains frame relationships; RViz displays robot models, measured and commanded paths, point clouds, arrows, and custom marker or triangle meshes that can encode ellipsoids. It can serve as the live display layer for AprilTag-derived TCP samples and path-error overlays. pytransform3d’s `TransformManager` is explicitly inspired by ROS `tf`. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009) | No dedicated peer-reviewed accuracy-map implementation was established in the retrieved evidence; related transformation and uncertainty functionality is documented by Fabisch & Popescu (2026), [doi:10.3389/frobt.2026.1860457](https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2026.1860457) | Open source and well suited to live experiments. Ellipsoid fitting, confidence scaling, and repeatability statistics must be calculated in a separate node; RViz primarily renders the resulting markers. |
| **MATLAB Robotics Toolbox / NumPy + SciPy** | MATLAB or Python | General-purpose implementation route for forward kinematics, Jacobians, covariance estimation, eigendecomposition, Monte Carlo sampling, RMS/P95 statistics, interpolation, and ellipsoid meshes. The core operations are Σₓ = JΣqJᵀ and Σ = VDVᵀ, with confidence semi-axes derived from √λ. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000030) | The retrieved literature supports the underlying workflow in Makhambetov et al. (2026), [doi:10.3390/electronics15143095](https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15143095), and Issametova et al. (2026), [doi:10.3390/math14030580](https://doi.org/10.3390/math14030580) | NumPy/SciPy are open source; MATLAB and some toolboxes require licenses. No retrieved paper establishes a one-click repeatability-map function in either stack—the analysis must be assembled from their numerical and plotting primitives. |


*Table: Software and computational frameworks for turning measured or modeled robot-position errors into ellipsoids, workspace maps, and trajectory-error displays. The notes distinguish turnkey visualization features from tools that require custom statistical processing.*

info.query:
We have a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. We want to place these arms in the published literature and compare them with industrial and research arms (e.g. UR5e, Franka, ABB YuMi, Kinova) using tests we can repeat ourselves.

(Lower priority) Visualizing repeatability: What methods and software show a robot's positioning accuracy and repeatability in 3D (error ellipsoids, repeatability maps, error along a path), computed from measurements or robot parameters?

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. For each benchmark or result, describe the protocol in enough detail to repeat it (what is measured, number of trials, success criterion, measuring tool) and give the arm model. For each claim, give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.
